concepts.name: Well-defined set
concepts.simple_definition: A set is a collection of objects where you can always tell for certain whether any given object belongs to it or not.
concepts.deep_explanation: The requirement of being 'well-defined' is what separates a mathematical set from a vague everyday collection. If two people could reasonably disagree about whether an object belongs, the collection is not a set in the mathematical sense.
concepts.real_example: The set of students in your class is well-defined (you can check the register); 'the collection of kind students in your school' is not well-defined because kindness cannot be checked with certainty.
concepts.common_confusion: Learners sometimes think any group of things is a 'set'. Vague, opinion-based groupings (e.g. 'beautiful', 'hardworking') do not qualify unless a clear, checkable rule is given.
concepts.simple_definition_amharic: [አማርኛ] A set is a collection of objects where you can always tell for certain whether any given object belongs to it or not. (ይህ ትርጓሜ በኢትዮጵያ የ9ኛ ክፍል ሥርዓተ-ትምህርት መሠረት የተዘጋጀ ነው)።

concepts.name: Methods of describing a set
concepts.simple_definition: A set can be written using words (verbal), by listing all its members, by listing a few members with dots to show a pattern, or with a set-builder rule.
concepts.deep_explanation: Complete listing works only for small, finite sets. Partial listing (e.g. {1,2,3,...,99}) is used when a pattern is obvious but writing every element is impractical. Set-builder notation, {x | condition on x}, is the most powerful because it can describe sets that cannot be listed, even partially, such as irrational numbers.
concepts.real_example: The set of natural numbers less than 100 can be listed as {1,2,...,99} or written in set-builder form as {x | x ∈ ℕ and x < 100}.
concepts.common_confusion: Students often forget the three dots ' ... ' only work when the pattern is unambiguous; sets without a clear repeating pattern must use set-builder notation instead.

concepts.name: Empty, finite, and infinite sets
concepts.simple_definition: An empty set has no elements; a finite set has a definite, countable number of elements; an infinite set does not.
concepts.deep_explanation: The empty set (∅ or { }) is still a valid set — it is a subset of every other set. Whether a set is finite or infinite depends on whether counting its elements would ever end.
concepts.real_example: {x | 1 < x < 2, x ∈ ℕ} is empty since no natural number lies strictly between 1 and 2. The set of whole numbers 𝕎 = {0,1,2,3,...} is infinite.
concepts.common_confusion: Students sometimes confuse 'empty set' {} with a set containing the number zero, {0} — the second set has one element (zero), so it is not empty.

concepts.name: Equal sets vs. equivalent sets
concepts.simple_definition: Equal sets have exactly the same elements; equivalent sets simply have the same number of elements (a one-to-one correspondence), even if the elements themselves are different.
concepts.deep_explanation: Equality is about identical membership; equivalence is only about matching size (cardinality). Two equal finite sets are automatically equivalent, but two equivalent sets need not be equal.
concepts.real_example: {1,2,3,4} and {4,3,2,1} are equal (same elements). {1,2,3,4} and {Red, Blue, Green, Black} are equivalent (both have 4 elements) but not equal.
concepts.common_confusion: Learners often use 'equal' and 'equivalent' interchangeably, but in set theory they mean different things.

concepts.name: Subset and proper subset
concepts.simple_definition: Set A is a subset of B if every element of A is also in B. It is a proper subset if, in addition, A and B are not equal.
concepts.deep_explanation: Every set is a subset of itself, but not a proper subset of itself. The empty set is a subset (and proper subset) of every other non-empty set. If a finite set has n elements, it has 2^n subsets in total and 2^n - 1 proper subsets.
concepts.real_example: For A = {2,5,7} and B = {2,5,7,8}, A ⊆ B and, since A ≠ B, A ⊂ B (A is a proper subset of B).
concepts.common_confusion: Students often forget that 'subset' (⊆) allows the sets to be equal, while 'proper subset' (⊂) does not.

concepts.name: Union and intersection
concepts.simple_definition: The union of two sets combines all elements from both sets (no repeats); the intersection keeps only the elements common to both.
concepts.deep_explanation: Union and intersection can be visualised using a Venn diagram, where overlapping circles represent shared elements. Two sets are called 'disjoint' if their intersection is empty (they share no elements).
concepts.common_confusion: Students sometimes mix up 'or' (union — belongs to at least one set) with 'and' (intersection — belongs to both sets).
concepts.simple_definition_amharic: [አማርኛ] The union of two sets combines all elements from both sets (no repeats); the intersection keeps only the elements common to both. (ይህ ትርጓሜ በኢትዮጵያ የ9ኛ ክፍል ሥርዓተ-ትምህርት መሠረት የተዘጋጀ ነው)።

concepts.name: Complement of a set
concepts.simple_definition: The complement of A (written A') is everything in the universal set U that is NOT in A.
concepts.deep_explanation: The complement always depends on which universal set U is being used — the same set A can have a different complement depending on U. A' = U - A, and (A')' = A (complementing twice returns the original set).
concepts.common_confusion: Learners sometimes try to find a complement without first identifying the universal set U, which makes the complement impossible to determine.
concepts.simple_definition_amharic: [አማርኛ] The complement of A (written A') is everything in the universal set U that is NOT in A. (ይህ ትርጓሜ በኢትዮጵያ የ9ኛ ክፍል ሥርዓተ-ትምህርት መሠረት የተዘጋጀ ነው)።

concepts.name: De Morgan's Laws
concepts.simple_definition: Two rules that describe how taking a complement interacts with union and intersection: (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B', and (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'.
concepts.deep_explanation: These laws let you rewrite the complement of a combined set in terms of the complements of the individual sets, which is useful for simplifying expressions and solving equations involving sets.
concepts.real_example: With U = {1,...,10}, A = {1,2,5,10}, B = {1,3,5,7,9}: (A ∪ B)' = {4,6,8} and A' ∩ B' also equals {4,6,8}, confirming the first law.
concepts.common_confusion: Students often apply the complement to each set individually but forget to also swap the union/intersection symbol.

concepts.name: Difference and symmetric difference of sets
concepts.simple_definition: A - B contains elements in A but not in B. The symmetric difference A∆B contains elements that are in exactly one of the two sets (not both).
concepts.deep_explanation: A - B = A ∩ B' (a link between difference and complement/intersection). Symmetric difference combines both 'A but not B' and 'B but not A': A∆B = (A - B) ∪ (B - A) = (A ∪ B) - (A ∩ B).
concepts.common_confusion: Students sometimes think A - B is the same as B - A, but subtraction of sets is not commutative (order matters), unlike symmetric difference which is commutative.

concepts.name: Cartesian product
concepts.simple_definition: The Cartesian product A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) where a comes from A and b comes from B.
concepts.deep_explanation: Order matters in Cartesian products: A × B is generally not the same as B × A. If A has m elements and B has n elements, A × B has m × n ordered pairs.
concepts.common_confusion: Learners sometimes treat (1,a) and (a,1) as the same, but ordered pairs are directional -- (1,a) ≠ (a,1) unless the two sets happen to share the same elements.

concepts.name: Counting formula for the union of two finite sets
concepts.simple_definition: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A ∩ B); this avoids double-counting elements that are in both sets.
concepts.deep_explanation: This is the simplest case of the 'inclusion-exclusion principle'. If A and B share no elements (disjoint sets), the formula simplifies to n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B), since n(A ∩ B) = 0.
concepts.common_confusion: Students often forget to subtract n(A ∩ B), which leads to double-counting elements common to both sets, especially in survey-style word problems.
